summary: Extends IS-IS to support Traffic Engineering by defining new information that routers can put into link state packets. This describes additional details about the state of links, useful for traffic engineering computations such as choosing paths based on bandwidth. It replaced RFC 3784 and has been updated later.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5305 lets IS-IS routers advertise more detail about links and IP prefixes. The added fields support traffic-engineering calculations and control how prefixes are shared between routing levels.

subtitle: IS-IS link-state fields for traffic engineering, including wider metrics, bandwidth details, and loop-safe prefix leaking.

tldr.problem: The original IS-IS reachability fields offered a limited metric range and little information about link characteristics needed for traffic-engineering calculations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5305 defines extended IS and IP reachability TLVs, nested sub-TLVs for link properties, a traffic-engineering router ID, and an up/down bit to control how prefixes move between hierarchy levels.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3784 and has since been updated by RFC 5307 and RFC 8918.

today: RFC 5305 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3784. It has since been updated by RFC 5307 and RFC 8918.

sections.title: Sub-TLVs for More Routing Information
sections.content:
IS-IS routers advertise routing information in Link State Protocol Data Units (LSPs). Each LSP contains Type-Length-Value fields (TLVs), which let routers carry different kinds of information. RFC 5305 adds sub-TLVs, which are typed fields nested inside a TLV.

A sub-TLV has a one-octet type, a one-octet length, and a value. Receivers ignore and skip sub-TLVs they do not recognize. The RFC uses them to describe link properties used by traffic engineering and defines extended reachability TLVs with wider metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: An IS-IS message carries labeled fields called TLVs. RFC 5305 lets some TLVs contain smaller fields, so routers can share additional information without changing the whole message format.

sections.title: Extended IS Reachability
sections.content:
TLV type 22 lists a router's neighboring systems. Each neighbor entry includes a seven-octet system identifier, a three-octet default metric, a sub-TLV length, and optional sub-TLVs. Without sub-TLVs, an entry is eleven octets and one TLV can describe up to 23 neighbors.

The default metric is a 24-bit unsigned integer. A link advertised with the maximum link metric MUST NOT be used in normal shortest-path-first computation, allowing the advertisement to describe a link for traffic engineering without including it in the ordinary shortest path tree. Metrics at or above MAX_PATH_METRIC are treated as MAX_PATH_METRIC during traffic-engineering calculations.
sections.plainLanguage: TLV type 22 lists neighboring routers and gives each link a 24-bit metric. A link with the maximum link metric is excluded from normal shortest-path calculations.

sections.title: Link Addresses, Bandwidth, and Metrics
sections.content:
The extended IS reachability TLV can carry sub-TLVs for an administrative group, IPv4 interface and neighbor addresses, maximum bandwidth, maximum reservable bandwidth, unreserved bandwidth, and a traffic-engineering default metric. Bandwidth values use IEEE floating-point format and bytes per second. Unreserved bandwidth has eight values, one for each setup priority from 0 through 7.

The traffic-engineering metric can give traffic-engineering shortest-path calculations a differently weighted topology. If that metric is absent, those calculations MUST use the link's normal default metric. A router implementing traffic engineering MUST include the IPv4 interface address sub-TLV and include the neighbor address on point-to-point adjacencies.
sections.plainLanguage: Link sub-TLVs can report addresses, bandwidth, and an alternate metric for traffic-engineering calculations. The unreserved-bandwidth field reports a separate value for each setup priority.

sections.title: Extended IP Reachability
sections.content:
TLV type 135 carries IP prefixes with a 32-bit metric. Each entry includes a control octet with an up/down bit, a bit that marks whether sub-TLVs follow, and the prefix length. The prefix is encoded using the fewest octets needed for its significant bits; any remaining bits are sent as zero and ignored when received.

A prefix with a metric larger than MAX_PATH_METRIC MUST NOT be considered during normal shortest-path computation. This allows the prefix to be advertised for a purpose other than building the normal IP routing table. RFC 5305 defines no sub-TLV types for this IP reachability TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: TLV type 135 carries an IP prefix and a 32-bit metric. It sends only the address bytes needed for the stated prefix length, and can mark prefixes that have moved down the routing hierarchy.

sections.title: The Up/Down Bit and Traffic Engineering Router ID
sections.content:
The up/down bit prevents a prefix redistributed from a higher IS-IS level to a lower level from being advertised back up and creating a routing loop. A newly injected prefix has the bit set to zero. When a prefix moves down the hierarchy, the bit MUST be set to one, and that prefix may then be advertised only to lower levels. The bit is also set when a prefix moves between areas at the same level.

TLV type 134 carries the originating router's four-octet traffic-engineering router ID. A traffic-engineering router MUST include this TLV in its LSP, and it SHOULD appear no more than once. Implementations MUST NOT add a /32 route for this ID to the forwarding table.
sections.plainLanguage: The up/down bit records whether a prefix has moved down the IS-IS hierarchy. A marked prefix can only move farther down, which prevents it from looping back up.

sections.title: Registries and Security
sections.content:
The RFC identifies TLV types 22, 134, and 135 and creates registries for sub-TLVs of types 22 and 135. New sub-TLV assignments require documentation and approval by a Designated Expert assigned by the IESG. The document defines no sub-TLV codepoints for the type 135 registry.

RFC 5305 states that it raises no new security issues for IS-IS. It points to RFC 5304 for general IS-IS security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Registries record the meanings of the new field numbers and control future assignments. The RFC says it adds no new IS-IS security issues and points to RFC 5304 for general guidance.
